label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Dear Nana,

I wish I were sitting in the kitchen with you tonight. I wish I could have a cup of tea and talk about tomorrow, and then talk about something else for a while, because I’m sure there has been enough talk about boxes and furniture and who’s taking what. I’m glad Denise is there. Thank you, Denise, for reading this. Please do Nana’s voice properly if you get to any of her lines.

I’ve been trying to write this all week. I keep getting a few sentences down and then getting choked up and shutting the laptop. Which is a bit inconvenient, since I work on a computer and generally need to keep it open. There’s just a lot I want to say to you, and I want to get it right.

First, I’m proud of you. I hope that doesn’t sound strange coming from someone whose entire life you’ve been supervising. But I am. You chose Elmwood Terrace. You decided what you wanted and made it happen. I know choosing to go doesn’t mean it’s easy to leave, especially after fifty-one years. You’re allowed to be excited about tomorrow and still have a hard time tonight.

And I’m excited for you, too. The place looks lovely. I’m glad there’s a big maple outside your window, even if the parking lot is also part of the view. You’ll have the tree to watch when you want a bit of peace, and the parking lot when you want to know everybody’s business.

The crib league sounds promising, although I do feel someone should warn them. They probably think they’re getting a nice new neighbour. They don’t know they’re getting a woman who taught a seven-year-old to play and then spent the next eight years refusing to give them a break.

I’m still grateful for that, by the way. Possibly not for every individual loss. Some of those were unnecessary. But you taught me properly, and when I finally skunked you at fifteen, I knew I’d actually done it. You had never once let me win, so there was no reason to doubt it.

And then you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I don’t know if I ever adequately thanked you for rewarding my victory with baking. It was a very generous response to what I’m sure was an unbearable amount of gloating.

I asked for the crib board because I want us to keep playing on it. Someday I’d like to teach someone else, too, and explain that in our family you do not get pity points just because you are small and your feet don’t reach the floor. I learned from the best.

I’ve been thinking a lot about summers on Kathleen Street. Especially that little television in the kitchen, and getting to stay up to watch the Expos or the Jays as long as I dried the dishes. At the time I thought I’d negotiated an incredible deal. Looking back, you got the dishes dried and I got to feel as though I was getting away with something. Very well played.

I loved being there with you. I loved having a job to do beside you and a reason not to go to bed yet. When I think about those summers, that’s so much of what comes back: being in the kitchen, watching the game, drying whatever you handed me, quite happy for the evening to go on exactly like that.

And I think about the back steps. You out there at six in the morning with your tea. Me coming out to join you, and you not saying anything until the cup was finished. You could be very clear about things without actually speaking.

I appreciate that more now. At thirty-four, I understand that sitting quietly with someone you love is a perfectly good way to spend time together. You don’t always need news. You don’t need to make a whole occasion of it. Sometimes you just need somewhere to sit, and someone who’s pleased you’re there even if they’re not ready to hear from you until they’ve finished their tea.

That house gave me so much time with you. That’s what makes it hard to think about saying goodbye to it.

You raised half the family in that kitchen. I don’t think I could separate my memories of the house from my memories of you even if I tried. And Grandpa Walt is part of how I’ll always picture it, too. I’ve been thinking about him as this move gets closer. I wish he were here for all of it.

I’m going to miss the house. I don’t want to pretend I won’t, or tell you it’s only a building when we both know how much happened there. Fifty-one years is a lot of living. I’m grateful I got to spend so much of my childhood in it, and that it was still there to come back to when I wasn’t a child anymore.

But I don’t want this letter to sound as though all our good times are behind us. We have a visit booked in two weeks. You have a new room I haven’t seen in person, neighbours to meet, and a whole new group of people to beat at cards. I’m looking forward to finding out what you like about Elmwood, what annoys you, and whether the crib league is up to standard.

I also need to say I’m sorry I can’t be there tomorrow.

I know you understand about being on call. I couldn’t find anyone to swap that week, and I have to be here if something goes wrong. Everybody has told me it’s fine, and I do believe them. I still wish I were there to carry things and be useful and give you a hug before you go. It feels wrong to be in Toronto for such a big day.

You don’t need to make me feel better about that. I just wanted you to know that being away isn’t where I want to be.

I’m sure you’ll want to know whether anything broke. I still laugh when I think about Christmas dinner last year, when my pager went off and you asked if the internet was broken again, and whether I’d fixed it. There are people in my field who would take forty-five minutes and a diagram to explain what I do. You’ve reduced it to “Did anything break?” and honestly, Nana, that covers most of it.

I love that you ask me every time we talk. I love that you want to know how work is going, even when it’s a world away from anything you’ve ever needed to bother with.

And I have never forgotten the card you sent when I got the job in Toronto, with twenty dollars taped inside: “For pizza, you look thin on the computer.”

I had a job. I was an adult. I was apparently still in danger of starving unless you intervened through the mail.

That card meant so much to me. Moving away and starting a job can make you feel as though you’re supposed to have everything sorted out. Then there you were, making sure I had supper money. I’m thirty-four now and it still means more than I can explain, knowing you’re looking out for me.

I hope Elmwood is good to you. I hope you get settled in and find people you really enjoy. I hope you keep your Tuesday crib games with the church ladies and add some new opponents to the schedule. I hope that maple is beautiful from your window. Mostly, I hope you’re happy there. You deserve to enjoy the place you picked.

Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and I’ll have the crib board. I’m glad those things are staying with us. There will be familiar things to see when we visit one another, and plenty of reasons to say, “Remember when?”

But we don’t have to spend every visit remembering. I still want to hear what you did that week. I want to tell you what broke at work. I want to sit with you without having anything especially interesting to report.

I’ll be up the weekend of December 5, once my rotation is done. You can show me around, and we’ll sit in your new room and see what’s happening out by the maple. I’m bringing the crib board for our first game at Elmwood Terrace.

Don’t practise too much before I get there. I’d like a fighting chance, and you know what you owe me if I skunk you.

I love you, Nana. See you on December 5.
